- A new field on `Profiler`: rejected, an existing test destructures it exhaustively.
- Moving the `LoopProfiler` into `SimLoop`: rejected, it conflicts with the borrow in
  `publish_input_overflow(&sim_loop, Option<&mut LoopProfiler>)`.
- Rebuilding raw as re-stamped + epoch: rejected, impossible once the re-stamp saturates at 0.

**Risk:** a hand-built `ThreadsConfig` that sets `loop_profiler` and also wraps the step in a
recording `ProfiledSim::new` would record each input twice; this is documented on
`ThreadsConfig::loop_profiler`.

## #82 — Owned-path extension for the trace hooks

**Decision:** The latency trace is wired through the smallest edits outside the issue's path list:
`crates/pin_app/src/orchestrator/mod.rs` (`pub mod trace;`, a `trace` field on `SimLoop` with
`SimLoop::set_latency_trace`, and four `if let Some(t)` hooks in `set_epoch_ns`, `skip_ticks` and
`run_ticks_inner`: tick start, each delivered event, after the step) and
`crates/pin_app/src/orchestrator/threads.rs` (a `latency_trace` field on `ThreadsConfig` and on
`RenderConfig`, installed on the sim loop in `spawn_threads`, and one frame-record call on each of
the render thread's two present paths: `presented(..)` after the debug presenter's render, and on
the table path `presented_at(..)` with the stamp the playfield hook took, see "#82 — Owned-path
extension: present.rs playfield hook"). `lib.rs` is unchanged.

**Rationale:** The applying tick, its tick end on the SDL clock, the drain times and the bat's
first move are only known inside `SimLoop::run_ticks_inner`, and the present time only on the
render thread. The issue lists `main.rs` and the new `trace.rs`; the brief names these two files as
the declared extension. Without a writer installed every hook is a `None` check, so default runs,
headless runs and replay digests are unchanged.

**Alternatives:** Wrapping the `SimStep` (like `ProfiledSim`): rejected, the step does not see the
raw SDL stamp, the epoch, the drain time or dropped ticks. Polling the triple buffer from another
thread: rejected, it misses ticks and cannot attribute events to ticks.

## #82 — Latency trace CSV format and where the frame table lives

**Decision:** `--latency-trace <file>` writes one UTF-8 file, version 1: the event table (header
`event_seq,input,down,sdl_ts_ns,apply_tick,apply_tick_end_sdl_ns,prev_tick_end_sdl_ns,drain_sdl_ns,prev_drain_sdl_ns,dropped_ticks_at_apply,stall,move_tick,frame,frame_snap_tick,present_ns,frames_to_photon`,
one row per delivered button event), one empty line, the frame table (`frame,snap_tick,present_ns`,
one row per presented playfield frame; a backglass- or score-only present is not a frame), and a
two-line trailer: `# overflows: input=N move=N frame=N pending=N` (each counter exactly once) and
`# run_end_ns=N`, the SDL clock read on the main thread when the run loop ended, before the threads
were joined (the run's end in the trace's own clock domain; a render freeze cannot move it).
Integers only, empty for "none", `\n` line ends, all times on SDL's clock. The column rustdoc is in
`crates/pin_app/src/orchestrator/trace.rs`. Every button event is recorded (not only flippers);
only presses of inputs bound to flippers (`DedicatedButton` / `ParallelLinked` staging) are watched
for a bat move. Capacities: 65 536 input rows (and bat-move rows), 262 144 frame rows, 32 presses
watched at once, a 5 000-tick move timeout; overflows are counted in the trailer and the summary
line. `prev_tick_end_sdl_ns` is an extra column (beyond the brief's list) so a reader can see
whether the press was stamped after the previous executed tick's end (the first-tick rule) or
reached the ring after that tick ran. For a press with `stall = 1`, `prev_drain_sdl_ns` and
`drain_sdl_ns` hold the stall's start and end (the drains of the last tick before it and the first
tick after it), also when the press was applied in a later tick of the same catch-up batch.
`move_tick` is the first tick with a bound bat raised at least 1 degree (0.01745 rad) from the
applying tick's start in the energised direction ("#82 — move_tick: 1 degree in the energised
direction"); `frame` is the first presented frame whose snapshot tick lies in `[move_tick,
release_tick]`, `release_tick` being the `apply_tick` of the next release of the same input
(unbounded without one), and whose snapshot shows the bat raised at least 1 degree from the press's
applying-tick base in the energised direction, so the frame showed the bat raised while the key was
held (the angles are kept in memory for the join and not written). `frames_to_photon` stays the raw
count from the press. On the table presenter path `present_ns` is the SDL clock read immediately
after the playfield `queue.present` returned, before any reconfigure and before the other surfaces
are drawn; only on the debug presenter (no table, or a playfield the table presenter cannot use;
`--debug-overlay` does not select it) is it read after the whole render call ("#82 — Review round
1: present time and trace write placement kept"). The trace file is prepared on the main thread at startup and written on the main thread
after every sim, render and audio thread was joined; no thread that runs a tick or draws a frame
touches the filesystem (same class as the startup table load). The trace is written to a sibling
temp file (created at startup with `create_new` as the writability probe) and renamed over the
destination at shutdown; the destination is never truncated, so a hard-linked bundle is safe. A
destination that is the `--table` bundle file (same device and inode; a canonical-path comparison
off Unix) is still refused before anything is created; a value starting with `--` is an option, not
a path. While
tracing, the main thread prints `pin_app: latency trace: first frame presented` once the first
playfield frame was presented, which the driver waits for.

**Rationale:** One file is one artifact, and the verdict is a pure function of one text plus the
shutdown line. The sections are separated by fixed header lines, so a reader splits on them.

**Alternatives:** A sidecar `<file>.frames.csv`: rejected, two files to keep together and two
paths to validate up front. Writing only flipper events: rejected, Gate A3 and KP-043 may want the
other buttons.

## #82 — Windowed latency check definitions

**Decision:** Presses are down events of the four flipper inputs. `TICK` = 1 ms. `move_tick` is
the first tick at whose end a bat bound to the pressed input is raised at least 1 degree
(0.01745 rad) from its angle at the start of the applying tick, in its energised direction. The
run's end is the trace's `run_end_ns`.
- **a. Key to coil (REQ-LAT-004, REQ-LAT-005).** Windowed check a verifies (1) the applying tick's
  end is not before the timestamp: `apply_tick_end_sdl_ns >= sdl_ts_ns`; (2) the lateness bound:
  `apply_tick_end_sdl_ns - sdl_ts_ns <= TICK + 2 ms`, plus the observed stall
  `drain_sdl_ns - prev_drain_sdl_ns` for a press with `stall = 1`, and no more; (3) the coil delay
  bound: `move_tick - apply_tick <= 8` ticks (the press takes effect, its coil energised, in
  the applying tick; the bound is the tick count the 1 degree raise needs, measured below). A press
  whose bat never moved fails check a ("the bat never moved after the press was applied"), unless
  its `apply_tick_end_sdl_ns` is within `8 + 2` ticks of `run_end_ns` (the run ended before
  the bat could move). "The applying tick is the first executed tick that received it" is verified
  by the deterministic SimLoop tests (`req_lat_004_apply_tick_is_the_delivering_tick`, the proptest
  `req_lat_004_first_executed_tick_and_req_lat_001_frames` in `tests/windowed/main.rs`, and
  `--test input_epoch`), not by the windowed run: the sim pops every ring event stamped at or before
  the tick end, up to the per-tick input buffer of 256 events (`INPUT_BUFFER_CAPACITY` in
  `orchestrator/mod.rs`); eligible events beyond 256 are applied in a later executed tick (the next
  one, or later ones when more than 256 remain: the app input ring holds 1,024 events) (test
  `input_overflow_defers_to_next_tick`), so an eligible event in the ring cannot be skipped as long
  as at most 256 events are eligible in one tick. The trace has no receipt time to tell a late
  arrival from a skipped one; the rest is tracked in a follow-up work-unit issue: the platform
  forwarder's receipt stamp in the trace.
  Check a's coil sub-check bounds `move_tick - apply_tick`, where `move_tick` is the first tick
  with at least 1 degree of raised-direction bat displacement. It is a proxy for the tick the coil
  is energised, because neither `FrameStateSnapshot`/`FlipperState` (pin_core) nor `SimStep` exposes
  the coil state and #82 may not change a pin_core contract (R2). A coil energised late but within
  the bound of `move_tick` still passes, so the bound (`coil_ticks`, 8, measured maximum 6 plus a
  margin of 2) is kept tight. The exact coil-energisation tick is tracked in a follow-up work-unit
  issue.
- **`stall`** is 1 when the press was stamped at or after the start and before the end of a stall the sim thread observed (a
  tick that started more than 2 ms after the previous executed tick, or after dropped ticks) and was
  applied in that tick or in a later tick of the same catch-up batch (each was due when the tick
  before it started); a press stamped before the stall's start reached the ring late and keeps the
  ordinary bound. The row's `prev_drain_sdl_ns` / `drain_sdl_ns` are then the stall's start and
  end, so the allowance `drain - prev_drain` is the stall unchanged. It comes from the sim thread's
  own scheduling and the timestamp, never from the lateness; the verdict's allowance depends only on
  those two columns, so a wrong flag buys nothing.
- **Tolerance 2 ms** (main-thread forwarding plus sim wake-up). Observed on the agent VM with
  `LP_NUM_THREADS=2`: drain gaps of on-time ticks at most 1.29 ms (p99 1.15 ms), press lateness at
  most 1.46 ms over 144 presses. With `LP_NUM_THREADS=3` one press was 4.0 ms late (the main thread
  starved), which check a correctly fails.
- **Coil bound `8` ticks.** Measured on three 60 s head runs (agent VM,
  `LP_NUM_THREADS=2`; 160, 170 and 170 presses): `move_tick - apply_tick` was 4 ticks for 495
  presses, 5 for three and 6 for two; the 5- and 6-tick presses came about 100 ticks after the
  previous release, while the bat was still settling at its rest stop. The bound is the measured
  maximum 6 plus a margin of 2 ticks, so 8. The pre-#81 behaviour delays the move by hundreds of ms
  to a second and still fails it by two orders of magnitude.
- **b. Key to photon in frames (REQ-LAT-001, CI form).** For every press not stamped within 500 ms
  of `run_end_ns` (excluded and counted): `frame` is the first presented frame whose snapshot shows
  the bat displaced by at least 1 degree in the energised direction from the press's applying-tick
  base, among the frames whose snapshot tick lies in `[move_tick, release_tick]` (the next release
  of the same input; unbounded without one), in present order: the first frame that showed the bat
  raised while held. `move_tick` only selects the earliest candidate frame; the count does not start
  from it. The gate is the raw count from the press:
  `n_raw = frame - F0`, `F0` the last presented frame at or before `sdl_ts_ns`, and `n_raw <= 2`
  passes; a press before the first presented frame counts from frame index 0 (`n_raw` = raised
  frame index + 1; PR #146 review round 3, O1). Exactly one allowance: if the frame in flight at the press (`F0 + 1`, the first presented
  after `sdl_ts_ns`) was presented in `(sdl_ts_ns, sdl_ts_ns + bound_a + 8 ticks]` (`bound_a`
  that press's check-a bound), the count may start after it: `n_adj = frame - (F0 + 1)`, and the
  press passes when `n_adj <= 2`. The shift is at most one frame and is never given to a press that
  failed check a. The summary and check b's line print the raw max and p99, the adjusted max and
  p99 (the gated count: `n_adj` for a shifted press, else `n_raw`) and the number of "in-flight
  shifted" presses. A press with no move, or no frame that showed the bat raised while held
  ("no presented frame showed the bat raised while held"), fails. The trace column
  `frames_to_photon` is the raw form; the verdict recomputes it from the frame table and fails on a
  mismatch. The bat angles each frame drew are not in the file, so the verdict cannot repeat the
  angle test: it checks that the trace's `frame` exists, matches its frame-table row
  (`frame_snap_tick`, `present_ns`) and is a candidate (snapshot tick in `[move_tick,
  release_tick]`, not before the first candidate), and fails otherwise.
- **c. Real time (REQ-LAT-002, CI form).** `D * 1000 <= N + D` from the shutdown line, and `N`
  within 1 % of the run length in ms. The Low quality preset is not applied (it does not exist yet;
  REQ-LAT-006 belongs to another unit); only the worker-thread cap is.
- **d. Completeness.** No trace overflow, at least 100 presses, as many presses traced as
  injected, and no dropped input event: the shutdown line's `input dropped N` must be 0 (each
  dropped event is a missing trace row; the field is required, a line without it is malformed;
  PR #146 review round 3, O2).

**SPEC erratum (REQ-LAT-001, CI form).** "At most two presented frames from the event to the first
frame showing the bat moved" can be exceeded by correct code: when a present returns within the
key-to-move time after the press (the coil needs the applying tick plus the ticks to raise the bat
1 degree), the frame in flight at the press cannot show it, and the next frame read its snapshot
when that present returned, before the bat moved, so the first frame that can show it is the third.
Proposed SPEC edit: count from the first frame that started after the press took effect ("at most
two presented frames after the first frame begun once the press was applied"), or state the CI form
at the 99th percentile like the millisecond form. Until then check b gates the raw count with the
one-frame in-flight allowance above, counted and printed. Measured on three 60 s head runs:
5 of 160, 10 of 170 and 3 of 170 presses had a raw count of 3 (in the first run the frame in
flight presented 0.2 to 4.7 ms after the press, inside the deadline window); the raw maximum was
3, the adjusted maximum 2.

**Rationale:**
- **Raw count with one counted allowance.** The render loop reads the next snapshot as soon as the
  previous present returns, so the frame after F0 (F0 taken at the timestamp) never shows the press.
  The frame after that shows it only if the bat had moved by the time that frame read its snapshot.
  Gating the raw count keeps the SPEC's form; the single in-flight allowance covers exactly the race
  above (the in-flight frame presented before the press could have taken effect) and nothing more:
  it shifts by one frame at most, only inside the REQ-LAT-004 deadline, never for a late press, and
  every use is counted in the summary, so a renderer that is a frame slow still fails.
- **Frames must show the bat raised while held.** A frame drawn after the release was applied may
  show a bat already falling back below 1 degree, and a ball impact or a stop rebound can drop the
  bat below 1 degree after `move_tick` even while the key is held; a frame at the release tick may
  show the bat falling. So the join tests each candidate frame's own snapshot with the same
  1 degree predicate as `move_tick` (PR #146 review round 2), not the snapshot tick alone.
- **`run_end_ns` from the trace's clock.** The last frame's present time ends the run early when
  rendering freezes, which would exclude (hide) every press made during the freeze.
- **A press that never moved fails a.** A coil that never fires is the worst key-to-coil delay;
  only the last few ticks of the run cannot show a move.
- **The coil sub-check in a.** The pre-#81 bug delivered events to the step in the right tick, but
  handed it the raw SDL stamp, which the simulation gated again against epoch 0. So `apply_tick`
  (the delivering tick) was on time and only the bat's move was late (hundreds of ms to a second).
  Without this sub-check, check a would pass the bug.

**Alternatives:**
- F0 at the coil deadline (`sdl_ts_ns + bound_a + 2 ticks`, this unit's first version): rejected
  in review; it could absorb more than one frame when several presents land inside the deadline
  window, and it is not the SPEC's count.
- The raw count with no allowance: rejected, it fails correct code whenever a present lands within
  the key-to-move time after a press (the erratum).
- A p99 frame criterion: rejected, the brief asks for every press, and p99 over about 150 presses
  still fails on two unlucky presses.
- A larger tolerance in a: rejected, it would weaken the check on the main thread's delay without
  being needed at the chosen cap.

## #82 — XTest key injection with X keycodes, no SDL hook

**Decision:** The driver injects presses with XTest through `xdotool keydown/keyup` and the X
keycodes 50 (Shift_L, left flipper) and 62 (Shift_R, right flipper). Before the presses it points
the mouse at the window and focuses it (`mousemove --window`, `windowraise`, `windowfocus`; bare
Xvfb has no window manager). There is no SDL event-injection hook.

**Rationale:** XTest goes through the real X server, SDL's X11 event path and timestamps, the
forwarder and the ring, which is what a player's key press goes through. A test-only hook would
need a cargo feature in `Cargo.toml`, which this unit may not edit. The keysym form `xdotool
keydown Shift_R` was measured to also press Shift_L (each right press arrived as left plus right),
so keycodes are used.

**Alternatives:** An SDL `SDL_PushEvent` hook behind `cfg(test)`: rejected, it is not reachable from
the release binary and skips the X path. Keysyms: rejected (above).

## #82 — LP_NUM_THREADS cap

**Decision:** `LP_NUM_THREADS=2` in `windowed.yml` and as the default of `scripts/windowed/run.sh`
and the driver.

**Rationale:** Measured on the 4-core agent VM, one 60 s run each with the grey-box table
(dropped ticks of about 60 000; presented frames; check a):
- `LP_NUM_THREADS=1`: 30 dropped (0.050 %); 277 frames; pass.
- `LP_NUM_THREADS=2`: 8 dropped (0.013 %); 526 frames; pass, max lateness 1.46 ms.
- `LP_NUM_THREADS=3`: 20 dropped (0.033 %); 734 frames; fail, one press 4.0 ms late (main thread
  starved).

At 2, the dropped ratio is a seventh of the 0.1 % limit, the frame rate is about 8.8 per second,
and the sim, main, render and audio threads keep a core between them. At 3, the four vCPUs are
oversubscribed. 1 halves the frame rate without lowering the dropped ticks. The VM is shared with
other sessions, so the single-run numbers vary. The method is in DEVELOPMENT.md "Windowed latency
harness".

**Alternatives:** 1 (fewer frames, no gain in dropped ticks); 3 (late presses); unset (lavapipe
uses every core).

## #82 — move_tick: 1 degree in the energised direction

**Decision:** `move_tick` is the first executed tick `t >= apply_tick` whose end-of-tick snapshot
shows, for one of the bats bound to the pressed input, a displacement of at least 1 degree
(`RAISE_THRESHOLD_RAD` = 0.017453292 rad) from that bat's angle at the start of the applying tick,
in the energised direction. `FlipperState::angle_rad` is the angle relative to rest, signed like
the flipper's `sweep_angle_deg` (`pin_physics` reports `sign * q`, with the travel `q` from 0 at
the rest stop to the sweep at the end stop and `sign` the sweep's sign), so the energised direction
is the sweep's sign; `FlipperBindings::of_flippers` records it per flipper (the grey-box right
flipper sweeps -50 degrees, so it raises towards negative angles). Motion the other way (a bat
still returning from an earlier release) never sets `move_tick`. The trace's frame join takes the
first frame whose snapshot tick lies in `[move_tick, release_tick]` (the next release of the same
input), rather than carrying the bat angles in each frame row, so the CSV columns are unchanged.

**Rationale:** REQ-LAT-001 counts to "the first presented frame in which that bat has moved at
least 1°". "Any change of angle" counted sub-degree jitter and the return motion of an earlier
release (which could set `move_tick == apply_tick` with no coil at all). A bat raised monotonically
while held stays at least 1 degree above its base until the release is applied, so the
`[move_tick, release_tick]` join is exact without per-frame angles.

**Alternatives:** Four bat angles per frame row (a fixed array) and a join on the presented
snapshot's displacement: rejected, it changes the frame-table columns that Gate A3 and KP-043 read,
for no gain while holds keep the bat raised. Displacement in absolute value: rejected, it counts the
return motion.

## #82 — Windowed press schedule

**Decision:** The driver's presses follow a seeded plan (`press_plan`): each flipper key presses on
its own timeline (hold = 3 frame intervals, `KP_WINDOWED_FRAME_MS` default 125 ms, so 375 ms,
capped at 1 s, plus 0 to 170 ms of jitter; gap 100 to 250 ms), the right key phase-shifted so the
keys alternate and overlap; times in microseconds, never aligned to ticks; the fixed default seed.
The two solo screenshot holds (left after 10 presses, right after 20, each 800 ms with only that key
down) and the two rest screenshots stay. A step that runs late shifts all later steps by its delay.
The injected count is compared with the traced count (check d).

**Rationale:** Check b counts only frames that showed the bat raised while the key was held. At
lavapipe's 8 to 9 frames per second, the old 30 to 200 ms holds often ended before any frame read a
snapshot with the bat up. Three frame intervals leave a frame read inside every hold with margin.
Longer holds on one key would give fewer than 100 presses in 60 s, so the keys overlap. A fixed
conservative frame interval (8 fps) instead of a warm-up measurement keeps the plan a pure,
unit-tested function of the seed and the run length.

**Alternatives:** Measuring the median frame interval in a warm-up: rejected for now (no frame-rate
line is printed before the run; the fixed figure is conservative and overridable). One key at a
time: rejected, about 85 presses in 60 s.

## #82 — Review round 1: present time and trace write placement kept

**Decision:** (1) `present_ns`: since PR #146 review round 2 the table presenter path stamps
after the playfield present (`AppSurfaces::render_with_playfield_hook` calls the trace's hook once
per playfield slot, before the backglass and score slots are drawn), and since review round 3b the
hook fires immediately after the playfield `queue.present` returned and before a suboptimal surface
is reconfigured, so a reconfigure can no longer delay the stamp. The table presenter is used by
every run with a table whose playfield the table presenter can draw (the windowed harness
included); `--debug-overlay` only adds debug lines over the PBR image
(`TableRenderOptions::debug_overlay`) and does not select the debug presenter. The one remaining
limit, documented in `trace.rs`, the trace-format entry and DEVELOPMENT.md: the debug presenter
(`pin_render::SurfaceSet`, `Presenter::Debug`), used only when no table is loaded or the table
presenter cannot be used (`choose_presenter`: `table_set_accepted` false, e.g. the playfield offers
no 8-bit format), lives in `pin_render`, outside this unit, so there `present_ns` is sampled after
the whole render call (late by that frame's remaining work and, on a suboptimal surface, one
reconfigure); a present-time hook there is reported as a request, not made here. (2) The trace file is
still written on the main thread after every engine thread was joined, to a sibling temp file that
is renamed over the destination at shutdown; the destination is never truncated, so a hard-linked
bundle is safe. (3) A frame counts for the
trace (and for the readiness line) only when the playfield surface presented (`paced_by` of the
frame's statuses), never for a backglass-only present.

**Rationale:** (1) `pin_render` is outside this unit's paths, and the debug presenter is not used
by any table run whose playfield the table presenter accepts. (2) No thread that runs a tick or draws a frame touches the
filesystem; the main thread already does startup I/O (the table load) of the same class. (3) The
latency is about the playfield bat; a backglass present says nothing about it.

**Alternatives:** (1) Moving the clock read into `pin_render`: deferred to that crate's owner. (2)
An I/O worker streaming rows during the run: rejected, more moving parts for a file read once after
the run.

## #82 — Owned-path extension: present.rs playfield hook

**Decision:** PR #146 review round 2 adds one method to `AppSurfaces` in
`crates/pin_app/src/orchestrator/present.rs`: `render_with_playfield_hook(snap, on_playfield)`,
which holds the body of `render()`; `render()` delegates to it with a no-op closure (same statuses,
timer handling and frame counting). Review round 3b (D1) moves the stamp ahead of the suboptimal
reconfigure with internal plumbing only: `render_slot` and `render_direct` take an
`on_present: &mut dyn FnMut()`, which `render_direct` calls through the private
`present_then_reconfigure` immediately after `queue.present` returned and before
`configure_surface` on a suboptimal surface; the playfield slot gets a real hook (the private
once-only `PlayfieldHook`), every other slot a no-op. The public contract is unchanged:
`on_playfield` is called exactly once per playfield slot with that slot's status, before any other
slot's work; for a presenting direct playfield it fires with `Presented` at the present, for every
other outcome (skipped, hidden, occluded, busy, a presenter-thread hand-off, which has no present of
its own to stamp) once after `render_slot` returned with the returned status. No allocation, lock or
new clock source. No other edit to the file. The render
thread passes a hook that reads the trace clock on the playfield's `Presented` status
(`FrameTraceWriter::stamp_playfield`), and records the frame with `presented_at`.

**Rationale:** The review finding (B2) showed `present_ns` read after the whole render call can be
late by the backglass and score surfaces' work, which can move a press's baseline frame. Only the
slot loop knows when the playfield present returned; a hook is the smallest additive change and
keeps `render()`'s behaviour. #83 (KP-003) owns `present.rs` and has not started; it inherits one
additive public method and a delegating `render()`, and must keep the hook's contract if it
reshapes the slot loop: it fires exactly once per playfield slot, before any other slot's work, and
for a presenting direct playfield after `queue.present` returned and before any reconfigure. A GPU test of the hook needs real SDL windows on the main thread (a `harness = false`
`[[test]]` entry in `crates/pin_app/Cargo.toml`, outside this unit's paths), so the hook's ordering
is covered by the windowed run, the pure test of `stamp_playfield` and the pure tests of
`present_then_reconfigure` (order: present, hook, reconfigure) and `PlayfieldHook` (exactly once per
slot); the Cargo entry is reported as a request.

**Alternatives:** A clock read inside `pin_render` (the debug presenter): outside this unit.
Reordering the slots so the playfield is drawn last: changes `render()`'s behaviour and #83's
design space. Reading the clock after `render()` (round 1): rejected by the finding.

## Process — Dual-harness agent documentation (Claude Code and Gemini/Antigravity)

**Decision:** Support both Claude Code and Gemini / Antigravity across the repository's agent
instructions, subagents, skills and process documents, using a single-source-of-truth layout with
no git symlinks:
- `AGENTS.md` is the canonical root instruction file. `CLAUDE.md` imports `@AGENTS.md` with brief
  Claude Code notes; `GEMINI.md` imports `@./AGENTS.md` with brief Gemini / Antigravity notes
  (Gemini CLI inlines `@./AGENTS.md`; Antigravity loads `AGENTS.md` directly and treats
  `@./AGENTS.md` as a path reference without duplicating context).
- `.claude/agents/` and `.claude/skills/` remain the canonical Markdown prompts and skill
  procedures, updated to be dual-platform (Claude Code and Gemini / Antigravity model tiers,
  GitHub MCP or `gh` CLI, and harness-neutral paths).
- `.agents/agents/` provides Antigravity custom subagent definitions (with Antigravity YAML
  frontmatter and safe cross-surface tool lists: `view_file` and `run_command` for read-only roles,
  plus `replace_file_content` and `write_to_file` for `task-executor`) that forward to
  `.claude/agents/`. Standalone Gemini CLI does not load `.agents/agents/`; its main session does
  not run executor or verifier roles directly and uses `.claude/agents/` only through custom
  subagents mirrored locally under `.gemini/agents/`, as documented in `GEMINI.md`.
- `.agents/skills/` provides Gemini / Antigravity skill adapters forwarding to `.claude/skills/`,
  plus the Gemini / Antigravity-specific `pr-watch` skill (`.agents/skills/pr-watch/SKILL.md`),
  which stands in for Claude Code's `subscribe_pr_activity` / auto-fix loop by scheduling
  non-blocking check-ins (`/schedule` or a single async background check-in), addressing CodeRabbit
  findings, resolving threads itself, and driving PRs to CodeRabbit approval and green CI.
- `docs/PROCESS.md` P1, P4, P5, P6 and P7, `docs/DEVELOPMENT.md`, `docs/BRIEF_TEMPLATE.md`,
  `README.md`, `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/work-unit.md`, `.github/pull_request_template.md` and
  `.gitignore` (ignoring `.gemini/settings.json` for personal project-specific Gemini CLI settings)
  are updated for both harnesses (including T0–T3 mappings for Flash-Lite / Flash / Pro /
  maximum-reasoning Pro alongside Haiku 5.5 / Sonnet 5.5 / Opus 5.5 / Fable 5.2, and `gh` CLI
  equivalents alongside GitHub MCP tools).

**Rationale:** The repository previously assumed Claude Code exclusively (`CLAUDE.md`,
`.claude/agents/`, `.claude/skills/`, Claude-only model names, MCP-only GitHub steps and a
hardcoded `/home/user/kilohertz-pinball` path). Antigravity discovers `AGENTS.md`,
`.agents/agents/*.md` and `.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` natively, while Gemini CLI discovers
`GEMINI.md` and `.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`. Forwarding from thin `.agents/` adapters to the
canonical `.claude/` files avoids duplicating long prompt bodies and avoids git symlinks, which
require elevated privileges or Developer Mode on Windows (a first-class target OS). Antigravity
custom subagent frontmatter requires exact Antigravity tool names (unmapped tool names can hang
subagent startup), so `.agents/agents/*.md` declares its own frontmatter rather than sharing
`.claude/agents/*.md` directly. Because Antigravity has no built-in PR auto-fix or GitHub-webhook
subscription, a dedicated `pr-watch` skill gives Antigravity sessions a repeatable, non-blocking
check-in and thread-resolution procedure without touching Claude Code's native PR subscription.

**Alternatives:**
- Duplicate full skill and agent Markdown bodies in `.agents/` and `.claude/`: rejected because
  every process edit would risk drift between the two copies.
- Symlink `CLAUDE.md`, `GEMINI.md`, `.agents/skills/` and `.claude/skills/`: rejected because git
  symlinks break or check out as plain text files on Windows without Developer Mode.
- Use `.agents/skills.json` pointing to `.claude/skills/` instead of `.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`:
  rejected because Gemini CLI reads `.agents/skills/` directly and does not read Antigravity's
  `skills.json` discovery manifest.
- Mirror `.gemini/agents/` in the repository for Gemini CLI: deferred in favor of scoping
  `.agents/agents/` to Antigravity and documenting the standalone Gemini CLI workflow in
  `GEMINI.md`, avoiding unverified version-specific Gemini CLI frontmatter.

## Process — Initial-usable-build review rhythm (tests along the way, sanity review on boundaries, full review at M1)

**Superseded** by "Process — Gate reviews at phase and milestone completion" below.

**Decision:** While M1 — Play experience (`#79`) builds the first usable end-to-end playable
slice, split PR code review into three label-driven modes in `docs/PROCESS.md` P6 and
`.coderabbit.yaml`:

1. **`review:skip`** (default for routine M1 vertical-slice, rendering, parts, cabinet, art, UI
   and table-content chunks): no automatic per-PR CodeRabbit review. Every PR remains gated by
   Implementer + Independent Tester tests, `work-verifier` (`pass`, P5 unit gate + R12 visual and
   windowed evidence), CI `pr-checks` and `main` CI.
2. **`review:sanity`** (targeted mid-stream sanity review): required on any issue/PR defining or
   changing public interfaces, schemas or wire contracts (`phase:11-contracts`, `crates/pin_core/`,
   `contracts/CHANGE_REQUESTS.md`, SPEC Appendix A/B, cross-layer spines such as `#92` vertex
   format and `#99` room/scene split), concurrency/state-machine/timing loops (`#82`, `#83`,
   `#86`, `#103`, `#149`), `very-high` blast-radius / simulation-output changes (`#87`, `#113`),
   R11 untrusted-table security paths (`pin_script` sandbox, `pin_assets` zip/VFS, `third_party/`),
   and milestone gate harnesses (`#124` Gate A3). CodeRabbit runs in `quiet` profile with
   `auto_pause_after_reviewed_commits: 2`; blocking boundary, contract, concurrency, determinism,
   security and correctness defects are fixed, while cosmetic style and minor refactor nitpicks are
   deferred to `#153` (KP-064) or M2.
3. **`review:full`**: runs the cohesive full review pass over the working M1 build in `#153`
   (KP-064, depending on `#124` Gate A3 and `#149`, and gating `#125` final acceptance checklist),
   lands high-leverage cross-cutting fixes, and flips `.coderabbit.yaml` to post-usable per-chunk
   review (`auto_review.enabled: true`, `profile: chill`, `labels: ["!review:skip"]`,
   `auto_pause_after_reviewed_commits: 2`) for M2 (`#80`) and all subsequent work.

**Rationale:** Running multi-round full CodeRabbit polish loops on every isolated M1 chunk slowed
down reaching the first playable build (for example, PR `#146` accumulated 40 review events and
PR `#150` ran 8 rounds) while risking premature polish on abstractions whose real shape only
becomes clear once the whole machine runs end-to-end under Gate A3. Keeping all automated tests,
coverage floors, R12 visual/windowed checks and `work-verifier` mandatory per PR catches logic
and integration regressions immediately; targeted `review:sanity` passes protect the boundaries
that are expensive to change later; and `#153` (KP-064) gives the full review pass the cohesive
context needed to catch cross-cutting drift, duplicated logic and state-transition bugs before
flipping to tighter per-PR review for durable post-usable work.

**Alternatives:**
- Keep full per-PR CodeRabbit review (`auto_review.enabled: true`, `auto_pause_after_reviewed_commits: 0`)
  on all 44 open M1 PRs: rejected because per-chunk polish loops bottleneck delivery of the first
  usable playable build and create sunk-cost attachment to early module shapes.
- Disable CodeRabbit completely until after M1: rejected because contracts (`pin_core` / Appendix A),
  timing/concurrency loops (latency harness, present queue, snapshot latch, telemetry thread),
  simulation-output changes and R11 security boundaries are expensive to retrofit once many chunks
  build on top of them.
- Rely on agent self-review during M1: rejected; R9 (no self-review) remains intact, with
  `work-verifier` checking objective facts and CodeRabbit remaining the sole code reviewer.

## Process — Gate reviews at phase and milestone completion

**Decision:** At the repository owner's request, align the review rhythm with the owner's other
projects: no code review on routine unit-of-work PRs, and one cumulative CodeRabbit review at the
completion of each phase and milestone (`docs/PROCESS.md` P6 "Gate reviews"). This supersedes the
label-driven `review:skip` / `review:sanity` / `review:full` modes and the planned flip to per-PR
review in `#153` (KP-064).

1. **Routine PRs** merge on `pr-checks` (and any other PR workflow), green `main` CI and
   `work-verifier` (`pass`). No `review:*` label is applied and no CodeRabbit review is requested.
2. **Gate issues** are the last open `work-unit` issue of a `phase:NN-name` label or of a tracking
   issue (M1 `#79`, M2 `#80`), or an issue labelled `review:gate`. The gate issue's branch is
   opened twice: once against `main` (closes the issue) and once, review-only, against
   `review-base/<gate>`, a branch at the last reviewed commit, so CodeRabbit sees every change
   merged since the previous gate.
3. **No git tags (D39):** the reviewed commit is recorded as `reviewed <sha>` in the gate's
   `docs/RUN_LOG.md` row. The first base is `4113e42`, the last commit of the former rhythm (the
   merge of PR `#154`).
4. **`.coderabbit.yaml`:** `auto_review.enabled: false` (nothing is reviewed automatically),
   `base_branches: ["^review-base/.*"]`, `profile: chill`, `request_changes_workflow: true`; the
   Orchestrator requests `@coderabbitai full review`, then `@coderabbitai review` after each fix
   push.
5. **Close out:** the gate issue's PR merges only once CodeRabbit approves every review PR of the
   gate; the review PRs close unmerged; `review-base/<gate>` is deleted where the session proxy
   allows branch deletion (an undeleted base branch is inert).
6. **Granularity:** phases (`phase:*`), not only milestones, so each cumulative diff stays within
   what one CodeRabbit pass can review; oversized gate diffs are split into area review PRs.
7. **`#153` (KP-064)** keeps its cohesive M1 review after Gate A3 (`#124`) as a `review:gate`
   issue but no longer flips `.coderabbit.yaml` to per-PR review. The retired `review:*` labels on
   open issues, and review-mode notes in their bodies, are ignored.

**Rationale:** Per-PR CodeRabbit rounds were the main source of fix loops on unit PRs (for
example PR `#146` with 40 review events and PR `#150` with 8 rounds), while unit correctness is
already gated by Implementer and Independent Tester tests, coverage floors, R12 evidence, CI and
the verifier. A cumulative review at each phase and milestone keeps review where it pays off
(cross-cutting drift, duplicated logic, contract, timing and R11 boundary defects). CodeRabbit
stays the sole code reviewer (R9); only its timing changes.

**Alternatives:**
- Keep `review:sanity` on contract, timing and R11 PRs: rejected by the owner's direction that
  review happens only at phase and milestone completion; contracts are still protected by R2 and
  reviewed at the first gate after they land.
- Review on the gate issue's own PR against `main`: rejected because CodeRabbit would see only
  that issue's diff, not the phase's cumulative changes.
- Git tags for reviewed commits: rejected under D39 (the session proxy may refuse tag pushes).

## #82 — Trace commit after a failed run

**Decision:** PR #146 review round 3b (D2): option (a). Once the engine threads are joined,
`run_app` commits the run's latency trace (`commit_trace` in `crates/pin_app/src/main.rs`) whether
or not the run failed: a run that missed its run cap or had a thread join error still renames its
trace over the destination. The destination is left untouched (and the temp file removed) only when
the run ends before that shutdown commit point (a startup error after the sink was opened, a panic
or an early return before the join), because the sink is then dropped without `commit`. A commit
error is printed, merged into the run's failure and makes the run fail. Unit tests:
`req_lat_003_failed_run_still_commits_its_trace`, `req_lat_003_commit_error_fails_the_run`,
`req_lat_003_dropped_sink_removes_the_temp_file`. The earlier wording ("a failed run leaves the
destination untouched") was wrong and is corrected in the `TraceSink` rustdoc and DEVELOPMENT.md.

**Rationale:** The 60 s windowed workflow uploads the trace with `if: always()`; a failing run's
trace is the evidence needed to diagnose it. The behaviour already was this; only the text was
wrong.

**Alternatives:** (b) Skip the commit when the run failed: rejected, it throws away the diagnosis
of exactly the runs that need one. (c) Commit to a separate `.failed` path: rejected, a second
path to validate and upload for no gain.

## #82 — Trace file permissions

**Decision:** PR #146 review round 3 (C2, CWE-732): on Unix the `--latency-trace` sibling temp
file is created with `OpenOptionsExt::mode(0o600)` (owner-only from creation, before any trace
data is written). At commit, after the flush and sync and before the rename, when the destination
exists as a regular file its permission bits (`mode & 0o777`, read at commit time; setuid, setgid
and sticky are never copied) are set on the temp file, so the rename never widens access (0600
stays 0600, 0640 stays 0640). A destination that did not exist ends `0600`: a trace may hold input
timing, so the owner-only default is kept rather than the umask default. Setting the permissions
failing removes the temp file and reports the error; nothing is renamed. Off Unix both steps are
no-ops (behaviour unchanged). `create_new` and the atomic rename are kept. In the same round the
destination checks were tightened: a metadata error other than "not found" (e.g. ENOTDIR for
`trace.csv/` under a regular file), a missing destination ending in a path separator and (Unix) an
existing FIFO, which a write-only open would block on, are refused before anything is opened.

**Rationale:** The temp file was created with the umask default (typically 0644) and renamed over
a destination that may be 0600, widening access to the trace. Owner-only creation plus copying the
destination's bits keeps the file exactly as private as it was; std's `OpenOptionsExt`,
`PermissionsExt` and `FileTypeExt` need no new dependency.

**Alternatives:** The umask default for a new destination: rejected, a trace may hold input timing.
Copying the full mode (with setuid/setgid/sticky): rejected, a trace never needs them. Opening a
FIFO non-blocking: needs `libc`/`nix` flags (no new dependency allowed) and a FIFO is not a trace
file.

## Process — Manual and physical testing waits for final acceptance

**Decision:** At the owner's direction (2026-11-25), no session waits for a person to test
anything by hand or on physical hardware. Agents automate what they can (PROCESS.md P2), record
what only a person can check as a `[P8 hardware]` line or in the item's DECISIONS.md entry (both
feed `docs/HUMAN_ACCEPTANCE.md`), and continue. A pending manual or physical check never holds a
unit, a PR merge, the work-verifier's verdict, a gate, or a run. PROCESS.md P2 and P8, the
`work-issue` skill and the `work-verifier` say so.

**Rationale:** The owner reserves manual and physical testing for one pass once everything is
complete (SPEC §4 Phase 8), so the run stays unattended (D28).

**Alternatives:**
- Pause a unit until the owner tests it on hardware: rejected by the owner's direction.

## Process — Fable ask retired

**Decision:** At the owner's direction (2026-11-25), the Claude Code "Fable ask" (D42; DECISIONS.md
"Process — Fable ask kept") is retired, as in fineprint. The Orchestrator never asks the owner
about Fable allowance and never waits for an answer. `FABLE_ALLOWANCE` is `sufficient` only when
the session can read the account's usage limits and finds enough allowance; otherwise it is
`unknown` or `insufficient`, the work runs at T2 (`Opus 5.5`) and a `[Fable wanted]` note goes in
the unit's `docs/RUN_LOG.md` row. PROCESS.md P4, AGENTS.md, the `run-plan` and `work-issue`
skills and the `work-classifier` say so.

**Rationale:** The owner wants sessions never to wait on them; the ask could leave a session idle
for up to 30 minutes. `[Fable wanted]` notes keep a record of where Fable would have helped.

**Alternatives:**
- Keep the ask with a shorter timeout: rejected; any wait on the owner is what is being removed.

## Planning — Browser version

**Decision:** The browser (WebAssembly) version is planned as tracking issue #144 (label
`tracking`) with 29 work units, #159–#187 (KP-065 to KP-093), one per row of #144's "Work units"
table and in its order. They are in four new phases: `phase:30-web-prereq` (W01–W05, desktop
determinism fixes), `phase:31-web-engine` (W06–W18), `phase:32-web-shell` (W19–W25) and
`phase:33-web-ci` (W26–W29). Every web unit also has the new label `area:web`. Each issue body copies
its unit's deliverables and acceptance criteria from the spike design (`docs/spikes/web/DESIGN.md`
on branch `claude/amazing-carson-30j8t5`, commit `aaab0b7`; keep that branch until #144 closes).
W01–W05 stay under #144 rather than M2 (#80). The owner approved the SPEC diff as is (P8 `spec`,
PR #158). Units that depend on open M1 units (#128, #96, #97, #102, #116, #133, #129, #130, #101,
#84, #115) wait for them. KP-065, KP-066 and KP-068 start `ready`; the others start `blocked`.
**Rationale:** #144's "How to start" defines this procedure and the unit breakdown. The spikes
settled the work; the breakdown, sizing and dependencies come from #144 and DESIGN.md unchanged.
`req_coverage.py` traces all 72 SPEC requirement IDs, including REQ-WEB-001..026.
**Alternatives:**
- File W01–W05 under M2 (#80): #144 allowed this, but the owner chose to keep them under #144.
- Start the units before the M1 units they depend on: rejected, because those M1 units change the
  render, audio, input and menu code the web units build on.

## #160 KP-066 — quat_ops design

**Decision:** Every glam `Quat` operation on a simulation path of `pin_physics` (product,
`* Vec3`, `conjugate() * Vec3`, `normalize`, `length_squared`, `from_rotation_arc`: 12 calls at 11
sites) goes through `pin_physics::quat_ops`, plain `f32` code that reproduces glam 0.33.12's SSE2
results bit for bit (same products, same sum grouping, division rather than reciprocal multiply, no
fused op). The module has no `cfg`, so x86_64 CI executes exactly the code aarch64 and wasm32 run.
The 180-degree branch of `from_rotation_arc` builds its half turn from `libm::sinf`/`libm::cosf`
of `PI * 0.5` instead of glam's `from_axis_angle` (std `sin_cos`); the test
`half_turn_equals_glam` shows the two agree bit for bit on x86_64 for ten axes. A proptest
(20 000 cases, SSE2/simd128 only) compares every output with glam; a 100 000-input PCG sweep pins
nine digests recorded on x86_64 and asserts them on every target. The seam-test reference inputs
(`slope_scenario`, `spec_ball_common::scenario`) are built from libm half-angle sin/cos and
`quat_ops`; the five seam digests and the replay fixture `state_hash` did not move on x86_64, and
`RECORDING_TARGET` now asserts them on aarch64 as well.
**Rationale:** S7 measured that aarch64 diverges only in the ball orientation quaternion, through
glam NEON's 4-lane dot sum order, its reciprocal-multiply normalize and the fused cross product in
`Quat * Vec3`. A replica of the SSE2 code keeps x86_64 output (the committed goldens) unchanged and
makes the other targets match it, as D9 requires.
**Alternatives:**
- glam `scalar-math` on aarch64: rejected; it equals x86_64 scalar code, not SSE2, and 78 % of
  `integrate_orientation` results differ from SSE2, so the goldens would have to move.
- Route through the replica only under `cfg(target_arch = "aarch64")`: rejected; x86_64 CI would
  never execute the code that aarch64 ships, and wasm32 would rely on simd128 staying op-for-op
  equal to SSE2.
- Keep glam's `from_axis_angle` in the half-turn branch (as the S7 patch did): rejected because it
  reaches the platform libm; kept only if it had differed on x86_64, which it does not.
**Residual risks:** using glam `Vec3A`, `Vec4`, `Affine3A`, `Mat4` arithmetic or `Quat::lerp` /
`slerp` in the sim would re-introduce per-ISA divergence (a clippy ban is requested outside this
unit's owned paths); `f32::min`/`max` with ±0 ties and NaN bit patterns differ on aarch64 outside
glam, which no measured run reached (`pin_core::fmath` covers min/max). NaN payloads are not part
of the `quat_ops` guarantee.

## #83 — Lean settings: render scale and probe captures carried as data until KP-035

**Decision:** `LeanQuality` carries `render_scale` 0.5 and `probe_captures` false as data (unit-tested), and the one-time software-adapter warning states them. MSAA, bloom and motion blur are applied for real through `LeanQuality::apply_to_post` in `AppSurfaces::new`.

**Rationale:** `TableRenderOptions` and `pin_app` have no consumer for a render scale or probe captures (`TableRenderer` renders 1:1 to its surface and `pin_app` does not use `pin_render::raytrace`). The files that would have to change (`view.rs`, the post chain) are outside this issue's owned paths. The Low preset of KP-035 takes the data over.

**Alternatives:** Edit `view.rs` and the post chain to scale the render (outside owned paths, larger blast radius); drop the two fields (the issue lists them as deliverables).

## #83 — Secondary surfaces keep frame latency 2

**Decision:** Only the playfield surface gets `desired_maximum_frame_latency` 1. Backglass and score surfaces keep 2 and their present-mode rules (SPEC §2.2, D19).

**Rationale:** The issue changes the playfield only; secondary surfaces redraw on change and do not pace the frame, so a deeper queue costs them nothing.

**Alternatives:** Latency 1 for every surface (risks stalls on presenter-less secondary surfaces and changes behaviour the issue did not ask to change).

## #83 — Owned-path extension: DEVELOPMENT.md windowed check c wording

**Decision:** Update the one sentence in `docs/DEVELOPMENT.md` (windowed check c) that said the SPEC Low quality preset does not exist, because the app now starts lean on software adapters.

**Rationale:** Otherwise the doc would contradict what the harness now runs.

**Alternatives:** A separate docs work-unit issue (rejected: a one-sentence fix that belongs with the change that made the sentence stale).

## #83 — Owned-path extension: fix main's aarch64 clippy (spec_kp066_quat_ops.rs)

**Decision:** PR #191 gates `unit_vec_strat` in crates/pin_physics/tests/spec_kp066_quat_ops.rs with the same SSE2/simd128 cfg as its only caller, so `clippy (aarch64-apple-darwin)` on main passes again (run 45553059132 at be86349, from #160 / PR #193).

**Rationale:** PROCESS P6 lets only a PR that fixes a red main merge; the #160 session could not be reached and the fix is one attribute with no behaviour change.

**Alternatives:** Wait for the #160 session (rejected: blocks every merge meanwhile); `#[allow(dead_code)]` (rejected: hides genuinely dead helpers on SSE2 targets).
## KP-068 — Address-free pairs order and string cache (KHZ 34, 37)

**Decision:** The vendored Lua no longer lets a memory address reach table iteration order or the
API string cache (third_party/lua-src/KHZ_PATCHES.md patches 34 and 37, both unconditional), and
every non-MSVC target compiles Lua with `-ffp-contract=off`. Patch 34: tables, Lua and C closures,
full userdata and threads get a per-state creation id (`khzid`, from the 64-bit counter
`global_State.khzseq`, low 32 bits stored; main thread 0, counter starts at 1) and hash as table
keys by that id; light C functions and light userdata share one main position, so their chain
keeps insertion order (patch 25 charges long walks). Patch 37: `luaS_new` picks its cache bucket
from the string's content (see "KP-068 — String-cache hash over a bounded prefix"). This amends
"Orchestrator — 4.2 pointer-keyed `pairs` order": iteration order over table, function and
userdata keys is now deterministic, the same on every run and platform, but it remains an
implementation detail that depends on insertion and deletion history and on resizes, so the
authoring rule stays: "Do not depend on the iteration order of pairs/next; use an array or sort
the keys when order matters."
**Rationale:** Both were native run-to-run D9 violations (S8 F4, F5): the order of `pairs` over
object keys changed with ASLR and heap layout, and whether `tostring` of an object with a long
`__name` hit the cache (no allocation, no patch-4 charge) depended on the name's address, so
budget units and heap bytes differed between processes. The web build (REQ-WEB-005) needs the same
lines as native. Ids cost no budget units and change no charge constant. Real header sizes grow
(on LP64 `Table` 56 → 64 bytes; closures, userdata and threads fill padding); there is no logical
memory accounting yet (KHZ 33 is a later unit), so a script near the memory cap that holds many
tables reaches it sooner: `lua_backend.rs::emergency_gc_is_charged` (18 000 live tables, then
60 KB strings under the 2 MiB engine cap) now hits `MemoryLimit` before `BudgetExceeded`; a C
replica shows the live heap at its phase switch going from 1 841 015 to 1 985 191 bytes, and back
to 1 841 031 with only the `Table` id removed, so the test's margin, not the budget model, moved
(reported as a request; the test is outside KP-068's paths). GCC contracts `a*b + c` into FMA by default on
aarch64 (2 sites in the vendored Lua, both unobservable today); the flag goes in lua-src's own `cc`
call rather than in `CFLAGS` for the reason given in "Orchestrator — 4.2 review: patched vendored
Lua". Production replays do not move (replay-hash fixture `state_hash` `25097c21c2c3adc1` before
and after; pin_sim and pin_app replay, autoplay and rules pins unchanged).
**Measurement (patch 37, worst case):** a `__name` of 64 KiB − 64 bytes pushed by `tostring` in a
loop until the budget aborts, release C build of the vendored Lua (`gcc -O2`), count hook every
1 000 instructions as in `pin_script`, best of 7, x86_64 container. Per callback: engine budget
(100 000): before 3.0–3.4 ms, after 4.6 ms; default budget (1 000 000): before 29–48 ms, after
39 ms (2 571 and 25 657 calls; units identical before and after). Short names (41 bytes): +0.1 µs
per call (engine budget 0.32 → 0.56 ms). Hashing the whole string instead, as first proposed,
measured 236–239 ms at the engine budget and 2.35–2.39 s at the default budget.
**Alternatives:**
- Keep address hashing and only document it (the 4.2 decision): rejected; D9 and the web build
  need one order on every run.
- A deterministic allocator instead of ids: much larger, and the browser allocator differs anyway.
- Hash light C functions by a registration index: no stable index exists for library functions;
  one shared main position keeps insertion order, and the sandbox reaches about 110 of them.
- Knobs (`KHZ_KEY_ORDER`, `KHZ_S8_FIXES`) as in the spike: rejected; one build, one behaviour.

## KP-068 — String-cache hash over a bounded prefix

**Decision:** `luaS_new`'s bucket is `luaS_hash(str, n, seed) % STRCACHE_N` with `n` the string's
length capped at 64 bytes (`KHZ_CACHE_PREFIX`): for strings up to 64 bytes it is exactly the
brief's `luaS_hash(str, strlen(str), seed)`, for longer ones the hash of the first 64 bytes. A hit
still costs one `strcmp`; `strlen` runs on a miss only, as before.
**Rationale:** The brief's formula hashes the whole string on every call. Its serial byte loop
costs about 60 times a `strcmp` of the same string, and a cache hit is uncharged, so `tostring` of
an object with a 64 KiB `__name` stalled a callback for 236 ms at the engine budget (2.4 s at the
default budget), against the binding 8 ms target of "Orchestrator — 4.2 re-review round 3". The
brief forbids a new charge (it would change budget units); a bounded hash keeps the units model
and the address-free property (the bucket is a function of content only) and costs +1.2 ms at the
engine budget (4.6 ms, measurement in the section above). Strings sharing a 64-byte prefix share a
bucket; they then miss more often, and each miss is charged by patch 4 as before.
**Alternatives:**
- Whole-string `luaS_hash` as briefed: rejected for the stall above.
- Hash the length and both 32-byte ends: needs `strlen` on every hit (measured 6.2 ms at the
  engine budget, close to the 8 ms target).
- A new charge per hashed byte: forbidden by the brief (changes budget units).

## KP-068 tests — Black-box observables for address-free order and string cache

**Decision:** `crates/pin_script/tests/spec_lua_addr_free.rs` observes KHZ 34 through integer
digests of `pairs` order (values folded in visit order) and KHZ 37 through budget units, meaning
the smallest `instruction_budget` at which a fresh backend loads the probe and runs one tick
without a fault (binary search over 1..4 000 000), plus `used_memory()` after the chunk and after
each of four ticks. The order script stores its 27 result slots in a Lua table and pages them out
through `on_switch(page)`, because `HostCommandQueue::persist_writes` holds 8 writes per callback.
"Different heap layouts" are made by live Rust-side allocations of pseudo-random sizes before and
between backend constructions and ticks. The string-cache probe runs in two name styles: the
spike's (names share their first 64+ bytes) and one whose names differ in their first bytes, so a
content-derived cache index spreads them. The creation-order variants (forward, reverse, stride 37)
run identical bytecode over a 60-entry permutation literal into a pre-sized `objs` array, so only
the order of string creation differs: a first draft with three different loops and an unsized
`objs` differed by 104 bytes of `used_memory()` on the patched tree from chunk code size and
table shape alone, with equal units. The order regression pin is an FNV-1a 64 of the order
transcript recorded from the first patched-tree run.
**Rationale:** The brief allows units by budget search "or any better black-box observable"; the
search resolves single charges (unpatched runs differ by 4 to 40 units) and needs no new API.
Paging keeps every result visible without overflowing the queue (an overflow would also count as
a determinism-unrelated failure). The second name style keeps the probe meaningful whatever
bucket function the implementation chooses, since the test asserts equality, not a hit rate.
**Alternatives:**
- Lamp intensities as the output channel: `f32` loses digest bits.
- One combined digest per tick: hides which key type regressed.
- Measuring units from the tick alone: the chunk's own cost is constant across runs, so including
  it changes no comparison and avoids a second budget path.

## KP-068 — emergency_gc_is_charged sizing after KHZ 34

**Decision:** The scenario sizing of `emergency_gc_is_charged` (`crates/pin_script/tests/lua_backend.rs`,
review B11) changes from 3000 one-element tables per tick with a phase switch at
`collectgarbage('count') > 1700` to 2000 tables per tick with the switch at `> 1450` (KiB). The
config (`LuaConfig::engine()`: 100 000 instructions, 2 MiB cap), the 30 x `string.rep('x', 60000)`
attack and the assertion `Some(&ScriptError::BudgetExceeded)` are unchanged.
**Rationale:** KHZ 34 added an id field to the Lua Table struct (56 B to 64 B on x86_64), and the
cap is still counted in real allocator bytes. The Implementer's C replica measured the live heap at
the old switch as 1 841 015 B before KHZ 34 (BudgetExceeded first) and 1 985 191 B after it (out
of memory first). Measured in the test itself on the patched tree, the old sizing reaches
~2.0 MB and faults with MemoryLimit. The heap grows in steps (1 419 345 B after 14 000 tables,
1 579 451 B after 16 000) and jumps to ~2.0 MB once `keep`'s array part doubles past 16 384
slots, so the switch must happen at or before 16 000 tables. With the new sizing it happens at
16 000 tables and 1 579 451 B, which is 517 701 B below the 2 MiB cap (room for several 60 KB
strings plus GC slack). The 1450 KiB (1 484 800 B) threshold sits ~65 KB above the previous tick's
heap and ~95 KB below the switch heap. With the default 200% GC pause the next normal cycle would
be due at ~3.2 MB, beyond the cap, so every collection the strings force is an emergency one.
Measured, the same attack faults with BudgetExceeded from a ~1.1 MB live heap up and runs clean
at ~0.65 MB and below and on an empty heap. Without the string loop the scenario does not fault.
On origin/main's lua-src (56 B Table) the new sizing switches at 18 000 tables and 1 857 139 B
(240 013 B below the cap), the same regime as before, and the test also passes there. The
assertion was not wrong; only the sizing had moved onto the cap.
**Alternatives:**
- Change the production code or the Lua Table layout: rejected; KHZ 34 is intended.
- Raise the cap or the budget: rejected; it changes what the test proves (R10, R11).
- Wait for KHZ 33 logical LP64 accounting (W10 / #168), which removes the dependence on the real
  header size: deferred; re-check this test's sizing when that lands.
## #161 KP-067 — Float min/max bans cover tests; narrow allows only for std reference checks

**Decision:** The `f32::min`, `f32::max`, `f64::min`, `f64::max` entries in each sim crate's
`clippy.toml` apply to every target (`clippy --all-targets`), so float min/max in tests and
benches is converted to `pin_core::fmath` like library code, with operand order unchanged.
Integer, `Ord`, iterator and `Duration` `min`/`max` and `f32::clamp` are deliberately untouched
(the lint only fires on the float methods, so the clippy output is the site list). Where a test
must call std `min`/`max` as the reference value (the CR-010 checks that `fmath` equals std on
x86_64), the item carries `#[allow(clippy::disallowed_methods, reason = "...")]` on the smallest
item: a single test fn, or the `#[cfg(target_arch = "x86_64")]` block inside a proptest body.
Part A has 10 such allows, all in `pin_core` (`src/fmath.rs` tests: 3; `tests/fmath_props.rs`: 7).
**Rationale:** The same `disallowed-methods` lint also carries the libm transcendental bans, so a
module-, file- or crate-wide allow would silently lift those too. Tests that run the sim must
compute the same bits on every target, so they get no exemption.
**Alternatives:** exempting test targets via `cfg_attr(test, allow(...))` at crate level
(rejected: hides libm bans in tests); leaving tests on std min/max (rejected: aarch64 and wasm32
test results could differ from x86_64 on zero ties).

## #161 KP-067 — glam bans in pin_sim and pin_assets; glam Vec2/Vec3 min/max premise corrected

**Decision:** In `pin_sim` and `pin_assets` (the Part A crates that depend on glam) `clippy.toml`
gains `disallowed-types` for `glam::Vec3A`, `glam::Vec4`, `glam::Affine3A`, `glam::Mat3A`,
`glam::DVec4` (both) and `glam::Mat4` (`pin_assets` only: `pin_sim` still builds collider
vertices with `Mat4::from_cols_array_2d(..).transform_point3(..)` at load time, so it is not
banned there), and `disallowed-methods` for `glam::Quat::{lerp, slerp, normalize, length_squared,
length, from_rotation_arc, mul_vec3, mul_quat, conjugate}` (plus `glam::Quat::inverse` in
`pin_assets`; dropped in `pin_sim` because `tests/backbox_colliders.rs` still calls
`frame.rotation.inverse()`), `glam::{Vec3A, Vec4}::{min, max, clamp}` and
`glam::{Vec2, Vec3, DVec2, DVec3}::{min, max, clamp, min_element, max_element}`. Every path was
taken from the glam 0.33.12 registry source and resolves (no clippy "does not refer to an
existing item" warning under `-D warnings`); none was dropped as unresolvable. The glam
vector min/max uses in `pin_sim` (`load::Bounds::add`, `escape_with_backbox`,
`autoplay::monitor::outside_distance`, 8 calls) are rewritten component-wise with
`pin_core::fmath`, operand order preserved; `pin_assets` had none.
**Rationale:** The brief assumed glam's scalar `Vec3::min`/`max` call `f32::min`/`max`. In glam
0.33.12 they are plain comparisons (`if self.x < rhs.x { self.x } else { rhs.x }`;
`min_element` is `min(x, min(y, z))` with the same closure), so they were already target
independent and, for non-NaN inputs, return exactly what `fmath` returns (a tie yields the
second operand in both). Converting and banning anyway follows the brief's rule that every float
min/max goes through `fmath` and guards against a future glam version switching to std or SIMD
min/max; x86_64 output is unchanged (replay fixture hash 25097c21c2c3adc1, see the PR). Only NaN
operands differ (glam returns the second operand, `fmath` the non-NaN one); no golden hashes a NaN.
**Alternatives:** leave glam `Vec3` min/max unbanned because they are comparison-only (rejected:
a later glam bump could change that silently); ban `Mat4` in `pin_sim` and rewrite the load-time
mesh transform in scalar code (rejected here: outside "only the min/max call form changes"; the
aarch64 fixture run in Part C covers this path).

## #161 KP-067 — Canonical NaN in the sim hash; which hashed floats are routed

**Decision:** `pin_sim::hash::Fnv64::write_f32` feeds `0x7fc0_0000` for every `f32` NaN and the
new `write_f64` feeds `0x7ff8_0000_0000_0000` for every `f64` NaN (positive quiet, no payload:
the pattern aarch64 and wasm32 produce and Rust's `f32::NAN`/`f64::NAN`); every other value,
including `-0.0`, infinities and subnormals, is fed as its exact little-endian bits as before.
`Simulation::state_hash` already feeds all its floats through `write_f32`, so it is covered.
The other float-bit sites that reach `fnv1a64` are the replay file writers
(`replay/mod.rs` `Axis` value `to_bits()`, `replay/game.rs` nudge `dv.map(f32::to_bits)`): they
serialise file bytes and the checksum covers those bytes for integrity, so they are left as raw
bits (canonicalising would change the file format and break NaN round trips); both readers
already reject non-finite values, so no NaN reaches a recording. `pin_core` and `pin_physics`
use neither `Fnv64` nor `fnv1a64`; the `pin_physics` test digests (the `quat_ops` sweep, the seam
test) use their own hashers and are Part B's concern.
**Rationale:** S7 measured different default NaN bits per target (`0x7fc00000` on aarch64,
`0xffc00000` on x86_64); S1 R-4 asked for one canonical pattern. No golden hashes a NaN, so the
replay fixture hash and the seam digests do not move.
**Alternatives:** canonicalise to the x86_64 pattern `0xffc0_0000` (rejected: sign bit set, not
the IEEE default quiet NaN and not what Rust's `NAN` constants or wasm produce); route the replay
file bytes through the canonical writer (rejected: they are data, not state, and NaNs are
already refused there).

## #161 KP-067 — Quat operator rule is a documented review item; pin_physics glam bans

**Decision:** glam `Quat` operator impls (`Quat * Quat`, `Quat * Vec3`, `Quat * f32`) and
`Quat::from_axis_angle` results cannot be banned reliably by clippy `disallowed-methods`, so the
"Quat operator rule" is written in the `pin_physics/clippy.toml` header and the
`pin_physics::quat_ops` module docs: in the sim crates, never use glam `Quat` `*` operators,
`Quat::from_axis_angle` results in sim math, or the banned methods; use `pin_physics::quat_ops`;
reviewers treat any `Quat` operator in sim code as a defect. `pin_physics/clippy.toml` gets the
same glam entries as `pin_assets` (`disallowed-types` `Vec3A`, `Vec4`, `Affine3A`, `Mat4`, `Mat3A`,
`DVec4`; `disallowed-methods` `Quat::{lerp, slerp, normalize, length_squared, length,
from_rotation_arc, mul_vec3, mul_quat}`, `{Vec3A, Vec4}::{min, max, clamp}`,
`{Vec2, Vec3, DVec2, DVec3}::{min, max, clamp, min_element, max_element}`), all resolving, none
dropped as unresolvable. Two `Quat` methods are not banned in `pin_physics` because call sites
remain that `quat_ops` does not cover: `Quat::conjugate` (`world/shapes.rs` `closest_cuboid`
feeds `rotation.conjugate()` into `quat_ops::mul_vec3`, and the `quat_ops` reference tests) and
`Quat::inverse` (11 test-setup frame transforms in `tests/`). Non-reference test uses of banned
`Quat` methods are routed through `quat_ops` (`ball/contact.rs` and `spec_ball_invariants.rs`
unit-length checks use `quat_ops::length_squared(q).sqrt()`, `ball_chain_pass_reset.rs` uses
`quat_ops::from_rotation_arc`, `spec_kp066_quat_ops.rs` builds its known-value input with
`quat_ops::normalize` and guards its replica digest with `quat_ops::length_squared`); the items
that compare `quat_ops` against glam's SSE2 `Quat` as the bit-exact reference carry a narrow
`#[allow(clippy::disallowed_methods, reason = ...)]` (7: 4 in `quat_ops.rs` tests, 3 in
`spec_kp066_quat_ops.rs`). The 22 glam vector min/max/clamp/min_element/max_element uses in
`pin_physics` src and tests (bounding boxes, `OBox::closest`, `closest_cuboid`, the seam
reference model) are rewritten component-wise with `pin_core::fmath`, operand order preserved
(`clamp(lo, hi)` as `min(max(x, lo), hi)`, glam's own order; `max_element` as
`max(x, max(y, z))`).
**Rationale:** Clippy sees method paths, not operator trait impls, so a ban on `Quat * Quat`
would be silent; a written rule plus review is the only enforceable form today. `conjugate` is an
exact sign flip on every target (only NaN sign could differ), and `inverse` is used only to set
up test frames, so leaving them unbanned costs no cross-target parity in sim output, while
rewriting them is outside "only the min/max call form changes". `quat_ops` reproduces glam's
SSE2 results bit for bit, so the routed test uses are unchanged on x86_64 (seam digests and
replay fixture hash 25097c21c2c3adc1 unchanged).
**Alternatives:** banning `conjugate`/`inverse` and rewriting the call sites as
`Quat::from_xyzw(-x, -y, -z, w)` (rejected: a refactor beyond this unit; candidate for a later
`quat_ops::conjugate`); a custom lint for `Quat` operators (rejected: needs a dylint toolchain,
not in the pinned environment); allowing instead of routing the non-reference test uses
(rejected: they are not reference checks, so the brief's narrow-allow rule does not apply).

## #161 KP-067 — glam bans in pin_tablegen

**Decision:** `pin_tablegen/clippy.toml` gets the same glam entries as `pin_assets`
(`disallowed-types` `glam::{Vec3A, Vec4, Affine3A, Mat4, Mat3A, DVec4}`; `disallowed-methods`
`glam::Quat::{lerp, slerp, normalize, length_squared, length, from_rotation_arc, mul_vec3,
mul_quat, conjugate}`, `glam::{Vec3A, Vec4}::{min, max, clamp}` and
`glam::{Vec2, Vec3, DVec2, DVec3}::{min, max, clamp, min_element, max_element}`), all resolving
under `-D warnings`, none dropped as unresolvable. `glam::Quat::inverse` is not banned, as in
`pin_sim` and `pin_physics`: four test-setup frame transforms (`src/backbox/tests.rs`, three in
`tests/backbox_outline.rs`) map a world point into the backbox frame with
`frame.rotation.inverse() * v`. The 33 glam vector uses (`DVec2`/`DVec3` bounding boxes in the
clearance validator and the ramp-entry zone, `DVec2::clamp` in the headroom check, `Vec3` box
bounds in the backbox generator, `min_element` in two test assertions) are rewritten
component-wise with `pin_core::fmath`, operand order preserved (`clamp(lo, hi)` as
`min(max(v, lo), hi)`, glam's own order; `max_element` of a `DVec2` as `max(x, y)`); the one test
`Quat::length` unit check uses `quat_ops::length_squared(q).sqrt()`. No narrow `#[allow]` was
needed in `pin_tablegen`.
**Rationale:** Same as the `pin_sim`/`pin_assets` entry: glam 0.33.12's scalar vector min/max
are plain comparisons whose ties already return the second operand, so the rewrite is
bit-identical for non-NaN inputs; it was checked end to end by generating the greybox,
apex_circuit and sky_deck playfields with the `origin/main` and the converted `pin_tablegen`
binaries (byte-identical bundles) and by running `pin_tablegen validate` with both on the 19
bundle fixtures under `crates/` (identical output).
**Alternatives:** banning `Quat::inverse` and rewriting the test frame transforms (rejected: a
refactor of test geometry outside "only the min/max call form changes").

## #161 KP-067 — Integer, Ord and iterator min/max deliberately untouched

**Decision:** Only `f32`/`f64` `min`/`max` (method, UFCS and function-value forms) and glam
vector min/max/clamp/min_element/max_element are converted. Integer `Ord::min`/`max` (`usize`,
`u32`, `u64`, `i64`, `Duration`), `Iterator::min`/`max` and `f32::clamp` stay as they are, and
no clippy entry names them. Per crate, float sites converted versus integer/`Ord`/iterator
`.min(`/`.max(` hits left: `pin_core` 9 / 4, `pin_input` 54 / 11, `pin_script` 2 / 17,
`pin_assets` 24 / 21, `pin_assetgen` 21 / 28, `pin_sim` 19 std + 8 glam / 32, `pin_physics`
542 / 70, `pin_tablegen` 140 std + 33 glam vector + 1 `Quat::length` / 9.
**Rationale:** Integer comparisons are exact on every target, so they cannot break cross-target
equality; `f32::clamp` is two comparisons with no zero-tie or NaN-selection ambiguity (it
propagates NaN on every target). Converting them would add diff and risk with no determinism
gain, and the integer min/max in the sandbox limits (`pin_script/src/wasm/limits.rs`,
`pin_assets/src/zip/mod.rs`) are part of the R11 boundary that this unit must not touch. The
lint fires only on the float paths, so the clippy output is the exact site list.
**Alternatives:** a blanket rewrite of every `.min(`/`.max(` (rejected: no gain, larger risk);
banning `f32::clamp` too (rejected: standing decision, it is pure comparisons).

## #161 KP-067 — One PR for all eight crates

**Decision:** #161 lands as a single PR covering Parts A, B and C (all eight crates, the
canonical NaN hash and the clippy bans), although the mechanical diff exceeds the brief's
~800-line guide for splitting.
**Rationale:** The Independent Tester's cross-crate clippy-bans spec test
(`crates/pin_core/tests/spec_kp067_clippy_bans.rs`) checks every one of the eight `clippy.toml`
files, so it passes only once all eight carry the bans; per-part PRs would either land a red test
on `main` or require dropping it from the earlier PRs. The diff is call-form rewrites with
operand order preserved, verified bit-identical on x86_64 by the goldens (replay fixture
25097c21c2c3adc1, the five seam digests) and by the byte-identical `pin_tablegen` output.
**Alternatives:** per-crate PRs with the spec test landing last (rejected: three PRs of the same
mechanical change and an intermediate `main` without the property the test checks).

## #84 KP-004 — Where config.toml lives

**Decision:** `pin_app --config <path>` names the file (a value starting with `--` is an option,
not a path, as for `--latency-trace`). Without the flag the file is `config.toml` in SDL's
per-user data directory, `SDL_GetPrefPath("kilohertz", "pinball")` (for example
`~/.local/share/kilohertz/pinball/config.toml` on Linux, `%APPDATA%\kilohertz\pinball\` on
Windows); when SDL cannot give one, `./config.toml` with one `pin_app: config:` stderr note. A
missing file means defaults and is not created until a setting changes. Load warnings are printed
one per line, prefixed `pin_app: config:`. (`ui::config_path_arg`, `ui::default_config_path`,
`ui::MenuController::for_app`.)
**Rationale:** Subphase 4.4 names no location. The per-user data directory survives reinstalls and
works for read-only installs; SDL already provides it on every platform the app targets, so no
new dependency. `SDL_GetPrefPath` creates the directory (only the directory, never the file).
`--config` keeps tests and the windowed harness away from the user's real settings.
**Alternatives:** next to the executable (rejected: not writable in many installs); the current
directory (kept only as the fallback); an environment variable (rejected: a flag is visible in the
command line and in the harness scripts).

## #84 KP-004 — Menu integration: save thread, running game, pointer, table loads

**Decision:** (1) `config.toml` is saved on the main thread, inside the `EventForwarder`'s
`forward` call that changed a setting (`AppConfig::save`: temp file, `sync_all`, rename), never on
the sim or render thread. A save error is printed once per distinct error and kept as
`MenuController::last_save_error()` (cleared by the next successful save); the change still
applies to the running app (`take_config_change` returns it). (2) The game keeps running while the
menu is open: `MenuOpened` / `MenuClosed` pause nothing; the sim only receives the releases
(`ReleaseToSim`, stamped with the toggling event's timestamp) and then no cabinet input until the
menu closes. (3) Pointer and mouse input are not forwarded to egui: the menu is driven by the
keyboard and controller through `MenuInput` on the main thread; the render thread only paints
the state snapshot it receives (`MenuShare`), at 1 pixel per point. (4) `UiCommand::LoadTable` is
answered with `report_load_result_for(id, Err(LOAD_NOT_WIRED))` until the table browser (KP-005,
#85) wires table switching, so the lifecycle never hangs. (5) The router's `HeldInputs` keep
tracking the physical keys while the menu is open (the platform module's held state is not
cleared on open; its API has no mutable access and `input_router.rs` is not this issue's): a key
released while the menu is open is consumed by the menu, after which the router and the menu agree
nothing is held; a key still held when the menu closes reaches the sim again on its next press
(its later release may reach the sim as a harmless second release).
**Rationale:** (1) The issue allows saving on the main thread because inputs are consumed by the
menu while it is open, so a few milliseconds of file I/O cannot delay a flipper; the I/O worker
has no config channel and adding one would touch modules outside the owned paths. (2) The issue
says the overlay opens "over the running game"; pausing would need a sim-side pause command (a
`pin_core` contract change) and is not asked for. (3) Keyboard and controller navigation is the
cabinet interaction; pointer support needs window-to-surface coordinate mapping on the render
thread and is not in the issue. (4) Table switching is #85's scope. (5) Follows the 4.4 routing
ruling (nothing is re-pressed on close) without editing the platform's held-input module.
**Alternatives:** a save on the I/O worker (rejected for now: no channel to it from the menu);
pausing the sim while open (rejected: not asked, needs a contract change); clearing the router's
held set on open (rejected: needs an edit to `input_router.rs`).

## #84 KP-004 — When each menu setting applies

**Decision:** Of the six settings the issue lists (code: `ui::AppSetting::timing`; rustdoc of
`ui::MenuController`):
- display mode (single / multi and the monitor indices): **next start**; the windows and surfaces
  are planned and created once at start-up from `AppConfig::topology_mode()` (an unusable plan
  falls back to one window on the first display, with a stderr note);
- PiP placement (corner, width): **next start**; part of the same start-up plan;
- score display (DMD / LCD): **no consumer yet**; the table's `backglass.toml` picks the display
  kind and nothing in the app reads the preference;
- input profile: **live**; the main thread replaces the keyboard router
  (`ui::keyboard_router`; `auto` = auto-detect; an unknown or keyboard-less profile keeps auto
  with a stderr note) and re-adds the open gamepads; the menu is open, so the sim holds nothing;
- staging mode: **no consumer yet**; the table loader does not apply a staging override;
- debug wireframe: **next table load** (at start-up until the table browser switches tables): it
  is ORed into `TableRenderOptions::debug_overlay`, which the table renderer reads when it is
  built; the renderer (`orchestrator/view.rs`, issue #91) has no live setter.
Every change prints `pin_app: config: <setting> changed; <timing>`. Camera preset is not in the
list (its consumer is the view, #91).
**Rationale:** Apply live only where an existing hook reachable from the owned paths exists; the
issue forbids inventing consumers outside them.
**Alternatives:** rebuilding the render surfaces or windows live (rejected: restructures
`run_app` and the render thread, outside the scope guard); a live wireframe setter (needs
`view.rs`, issue #91's).
